source.title: Making Your LLMs More Objective: Stabilizing LLM Safety Behavior Across Traits with Trait-Invariant Safety Tuning

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how system-prompt traits change harmful-request refusal and benign-request over-refusal, using refusal rates and trait-variation metrics. This is a different prompt manipulation from the fine-tuning, first-token, and bypass conditions specified in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study tests trait-conditioned safety variation, which is relevant to safety behavior but does not test any of V1–V7 as defined. The table results below are the untrained-model measurements; the study's own TIST/TraSN methods are not entered as rows because their comparisons are not tests of those versions. Cited findings from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study measures how persona/trait system prompts shift refusal and over-refusal (TID, TFR), plus activation shifts at a chosen layer. It then trains its own self-distillation adapters (TIST/TraSN). It does no harmful or benign fine-tuning to measure safety loss (V1, V2). It does not measure per-token KL or position-wise safety (V3). It uses no prefilling, suffixes or decoding changes; a persona system prompt is a different manipulation (V4). Its low-rank structure is a subspace of trait-induced activation shifts, not a small set of weights or ranks carrying safety (V5). It does not study why safety is shallow (V6) or test token-deepening training (V7). Qi et al. 2025 is only cited as a 'deeper safety training' defense. The reader's 'tests/T2' is wrong: no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that system-prompt traits, including benign roles and personality traits and not only adversarial roles, change refusal decisions on fixed requests. They find these shifts lie in a low-dimensional, safety-relevant activation subspace. Their TIST self-distillation, and especially the subspace-localized TraSN, reduces TID and TFR. TraSN also raises harmful refusal while keeping over-refusal and general capability close to the untrained model.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures trait-conditioned safety variation and trains self-distillation/representation-matching adapters; it does not use the harmful-example or first-token interventions in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The magnitude of trait-induced variation differs across model, request group, dataset, and trait. The study reports results across three trait families and both harmful and benign request groups; it does not give a single numerical result for each trait in the text.

fits_no_version.finding: Untrained aligned models show nonzero trait-induced deviation and flip rates on harmful and benign requests. Example: Gemma-4-E2B harmful TID 12.72, TFR 18.14; Qwen benign TFR 21.00 (Table 1). In the Appendix J case study, Llama-3.2-3B refuses one WJB-Harmful request with no trait but complies under 8 of 12 traits (Table 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Persona or trait system prompts, without explicit jailbreak instructions, change aligned models' refusal decisions on fixed requests. They lower harmful refusal and raise benign over-refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: Trait-induced shifts in last-prompt-token activations mostly move toward the benign side of the harmful–benign axis. A rank-4 subspace captures 77–79% of shift variance across the three models (Figure 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Trait-induced safety shifts are concentrated in a low-dimensional activation subspace aligned with the harmful–benign axis.

record.problems: The authors note that the study covers a representative, not exhaustive, set of models, traits, and deployment settings; uses linear representations that may not capture all mechanisms; and relies on refusal-based metrics and LLM judging, which may miss nuanced safety and utility. The listed results provide no error bars, confidence intervals, or p-values.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted due to the 60-row limit. TIST/TraSN intervention comparisons and the random-subspace comparison are not included because they are the study's proposed tuning method results, not tests of V1–V7.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples and no measurement of the resulting harmful compliance.
No benign fine-tuning measured for safety erosion. TIST/TraSN training on benign prompts is the authors' mitigation and is not evaluated as an erosion test.
No per-token or per-position KL between aligned and base models.
No prefilling, adversarial suffix or decoding attacks. Persona system prompts are a different manipulation.
No test of whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety. The rank-4 subspace concerns trait-induced activation shifts.
No analysis of whether the data or training objective causes shallow alignment.
No training that extends safety beyond the first tokens, and no test of its durability.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's own gate_note already said no version is tested, which contradicts its relation 'tests'. Relation is set to cites_only, tranche T6. The paper's remark that refusal 'can usually be determined from the opening response' is only a justification for the 256-token generation budget, not a test of V3 or V4. The TIST/TraSN and random-subspace results were correctly excluded from the rows.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune safety-trained models on harmful examples to measure harmful compliance.
Does not test ordinary or carefully selected benign fine-tuning as a cause of increased harmful compliance.
Does not measure per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions.
Does not test compliant response prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as bypasses.
Does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Does not test whether the data or objective used in safety training causes first-token shallowness.
Does not test training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens or whether such training holds up.
